items.title: In Strict Confidence announce ‘The Final Kiss’ album for 20 November
items.summary: In Strict Confidence announce "The Final Kiss," their first studio album since 2018, due November 20, 2026 via Minuswelt on CD and vinyl LP.
items.fullText:
German electro-industrial act In Strict Confidence will release “The Final Kiss,” its first studio album since 2018’s “Hate2Love,” on November 20, 2026, through Minuswelt. The album follows “Fever,” released as the lead single on October 16, 2026, with an official video and remixes by Controlled Fusion and Italian darkwave act Ash Code.

“The Final Kiss” also includes “Blasphemous Rumours,” In Strict Confidence’s cover of the Depeche Mode song, which the band released as its own single and video in February 2026.

The album mixes dark electro, driving rhythms and atmospheric arrangements, following the direction of “Fever” and “Blasphemous Rumours.” It is available for pre-order on CD, as a limited-edition clear, marbled vinyl LP with the exclusive bonus track “Digital Cage,” and digitally through the band’s official shop.

“The Final Kiss” tracklist:

  1. “Fever”
  2. “Heartbreaker”
  3. “Fallen Angel”
  4. “Blasphemous Rumours”
  5. “The Ocean’s Roar”
  6. “Fake Love Again”
  7. “Watch Us Fall”
  8. “Where Is Your God Now?”
  9. “No Secret”
  10. “Schattenmelodie”

The vinyl edition adds “Digital Cage” as an eleventh, exclusive track.

In Strict Confidence are performing live again, with shows already held across Europe in 2026 and further dates, including Austria, Germany and Spain, planned for 2027.

About In Strict Confidence

In Strict Confidence formed in Germany in 1989 as a quartet under the name Seal of Secrecy, renaming itself In Strict Confidence in 1992 after keyboardist Thomas Steiger left, narrowing the group to the duo of Dennis Ostermann and Jörg Schelte. Founding drummer Stefan Vesper also left in 1992 and returned around 2001, in time for “Mistrust the Angels.”

The band released its debut album, “Cryogenix,” in 1996 on Zoth Ommog, followed by “Face the Fear” (1997) on the same label and “Love Kills!” (2000) on Bloodline. “Mistrust the Angels” (2002) and “Holy” (2004) both charted on the Offizielle Deutsche Charts, and “Exile Paradise” (2006) reached number three on the German Alternative Charts. Heidi Pulkkinen, credited as HayDee Sparks, joined on guitars in 2008, and Nina de Lianin joined on vocals and lyrics in 2009, completing the band’s current line-up alongside Ostermann, Schelte and Vesper.

“La Parade Monstrueuse” (2010) and “Utopia” (2012) followed before the band moved to Minuswelt for “The Hardest Heart” in 2016, which reached number two on the Deutsche Alternative Charts. The band issued “Hate2Love” in 2018, followed by the “Mercy” EP the same year and a limited double-vinyl edition pairing the two. In 2021, the band marked the 25th anniversary of its debut with “Cryogenix (25 Years Edition),” and in 2023 reissued “La Parade Monstrueuse” as a 3CD set. Dennis Ostermann also records as Controlled Fusion, who remixed “Fever.”

Eight years after “Hate2Love,” In Strict Confidence returned in 2026 with the single “Fever,” followed by the Depeche Mode cover “Blasphemous Rumours,” ahead of “The Final Kiss,” due November 20, 2026, through Minuswelt.

items.title: The Berzerker reissue ‘The Reawakening’ on splatter vinyl October 30
items.summary: The Berzerker's "The Reawakening" gets a splatter vinyl, CD and cassette reissue via Apocalyptic Witchcraft on October 30, 2026.
items.fullText:
Australian industrial death metal band The Berzerker will reissue “The Reawakening” on limited edition splatter vinyl, digipak CD and cassette on October 30, 2026, through Apocalyptic Witchcraft. The album returned to digital platforms on July 17, 2026, after band founder Luke Kenny withdrew it from sale and streaming shortly following its original 2008 release.

The Reawakening was The Berzerker’s fifth album and its first released independently, following four albums on Earache Records: “The Berzerker” (2000), “Dissimulate” (2002), “World of Lies” (2005) and “Animosity” (2007). Kenny self-released “The Reawakening” through Berzerker Industries and sold it only through the band’s own online store before pulling it from circulation, after which the album circulated among fans through word of mouth and shared copies for nearly two decades.

Apocalyptic Witchcraft is run by Conor Droney. “Discovering The Berzerker on a compilation at 15 was a life-changing moment that set me on the path I’m on today. It is only right that The Berzerker would end up working with Apocalyptic Witchcraft. The kings of extreme metal have returned,” Droney stated.

The 2026 line-up is Luke Kenny (vocals, programming), Sam Bean (bass, guitars, vocals), Matt Wilcock (guitars) and Todd Hansen (drums). The reissue arrives ahead of the band’s appearance at Damnation Festival in Manchester, alongside Carcass, Crowbar and Satyricon.

“The Reawakening” runs ten tracks: ‘Wisdom and Corruption,’ ‘Caught In The Crossfire,’ ‘Disassembly Line,’ ‘The Deception,’ ‘Evolution of Aggression,’ ‘Your Final Seconds,’ ‘Harvesting a Loved One,’ ‘Internal Examination,’ ‘Spare Parts’ and ‘An Unforgotten Force.’

“The Reawakening” can be pre-ordered through Apocalyptic Witchcraft.

About The Berzerker

The Berzerker formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1995 around Luke Kenny, who coined the term industrial death metal to describe the project’s fusion of extreme metal and programmed electronics. Earache Records signed the band after remixes Kenny made of songs by Deicide and Morbid Angel attracted attention, and the band released its self-titled debut album in 2000.

Three more albums followed on Earache: “Dissimulate” in 2002, after Gary Thomas and Matt Wilcock joined the line-up; “World of Lies” in 2005, recorded with the original line-up and built entirely around programmed drums; and “Animosity” in 2007, which returned to the drum-machine-driven, faster-tempo approach of the band’s early material and became its last release for the label. Several of the band’s music videos were refused broadcast, and the band performed masked in its early years before dropping the masks after the 2004 DVD “The Principles and Practices of The Berzerker.”

“The Reawakening” followed in 2008, self-released through Berzerker Industries and sold only through the band’s own store. Kenny withdrew it from sale and streaming shortly afterward, and the band went quiet after October 2009. The group released a cover of t.A.T.u.’s “All the Things She Said” in 2020 and, after a planned album was postponed indefinitely in December 2023, returned with the video for “The Deception” in 2025. The Berzerker played its first live show in years at Necrosonic Festival on August 22, 2026, with the same Kenny, Bean, Wilcock and Hansen line-up now bringing “The Reawakening” back into print through Apocalyptic Witchcraft.

items.title: Bruce Gilbert sets ‘London Orbital’ vinyl release for 27 November
items.summary: Bruce Gilbert's "London Orbital" soundtrack gets its first vinyl edition via The Hotel on November 27, 2026, with essays by Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair.
items.fullText:
English musician Bruce Gilbert will release “London Orbital” on vinyl on November 27, 2026, through The Hotel. The album is Gilbert’s sound work for the 2002 Channel 4 film of the same name, directed by Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair.

The film follows the M25, the motorway that circles London, and takes its title from Sinclair’s 2000 book of the same name, which traced the author’s two-year walk around the route. Petit drove the motorway instead, using early digital video and CCTV footage to build the film’s imagery. In Gilbert’s album, the circular road becomes a device for “forward projection” and what The Hotel describes as “a quest for transcendental boredom and extreme impersonality.”

The Hotel presents the release as a sound film, not a conventional soundtrack record. The LP’s booklet carries stills from the film alongside new essays by Petit and Sinclair, and ships from around November 20, 2026, ahead of the full LP, booklet and digital bundle shipping on November 27. A 5-minute excerpt from the album streams now on Bandcamp, where the 18-minute “London Orbital Side A” is also available digitally; “Side B” is exclusive to the vinyl edition.

Gilbert recorded the music and sounds, with writings and voiceover by Petit and Sinclair. Emma Matthews edited the film version for television, and Henry Cyer, who also executive produced the release, edited it for vinyl. Petit and Sinclair supplied the artwork, Jon Wozencroft designed the release, and Kinn handled mastering. Cargo distributes the record, which carries the support of Arts Council England under copyright held by Illuminations Television Ltd, licensed exclusively to The Hotel.

The announcement follows Gilbert’s solo set at Café OTO in London on October 9, 2026, where The Hotel previewed an as-yet-unannounced album with test pressings sold at the merch table, the record now confirmed as “London Orbital”. “London Orbital” can be pre-ordered through The Hotel.

About Bruce Gilbert

Bruce Gilbert, born in 1946, is an English musician and one of the founding members of Wire, the London post-punk band. Alongside Wire, he worked extensively with fellow member Graham Lewis, including in Dome and in AC Marias. With Lewis and Daniel Miller of The Normal and Silicon Teens, Gilbert recorded “Or So It Seems” as Duet Emmo, the trio’s sole collaboration; Miller, Lewis and Gilbert played the record live for the first time in October 2026 at London’s ICA, nearly 45 years after it was recorded, as Side-Line reported at the time.

Gilbert has also released solo work through Mute, Touch and Editions Mego. In October 2026, Wire’s 1991 album “The First Letter”, released under the one-word name Wir after drummer Robert Gotobed’s departure and recorded with Gilbert alongside Colin Newman and Graham Lewis, marked its 35th anniversary. “London Orbital” now gives Gilbert’s standalone sound work for Petit and Sinclair’s film its first dedicated release, arriving on vinyl through The Hotel on November 27, 2026.

items.title: Sara Noxx announces ‘Ultraviolet’ from upcoming album ‘Onyxx’
items.summary: Sara Noxx has announced "Ultraviolet", the first single from her new album "Onyxx", set for digital release on November 6, 2026.
items.fullText:
German dark electronic artist Sara Noxx has announced “Ultraviolet“, a new single scheduled for digital release on November 6, 2026. The track is introduced as the first “Triple-A” release from her forthcoming album “Onyxx“.

Following the 2026 singles “Poor Old Man” and “Under Attack”, “Ultraviolet” takes a more direct, club-oriented approach, with a faster bassline, sharp synth arrangements and Noxx’s vocals, built for both radio and dancefloor play. Both earlier singles reached number one on the Deutsche Alternative Charts (DAC) and the American Alternative Charts (AAC), according to the artist’s own announcement.

“Onyxx” forms part of a three-part project alongside “Polluxx” and “Detoxx”, first announced by Sara Noxx in March 2026. “Ultraviolet” is set for digital release on November 6, accompanied by international club and radio promotion.

About Sara Noxx

Sara Noxx, born Britt Rommel, is a Berlin-based dark electronic and electro-industrial artist. She first appeared in 1997, winning the Zillo band contest with her project Essexx and releasing the debut single “Society” and her first studio album “Noxxious” the same year. In 1998 she issued the album “Paradoxx”. The 2001 album “Exxtasy” reached number 9 on the DAC; the 2003 album “Equinoxx” and the single “Colder & Colder” came next, with “Colder & Colder” reaching number one on European alternative charts for several weeks. The same year she released the instrumental album “Nonvoxx” and her first poetry collection, “Lyrixx”. In 2007 she relaunched Essexx with Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff and released the album “Bridges”. For her ten-year solo anniversary in 2008 she released the three-disc retrospective “XX-Ray”; the same year’s single “Earth Song” was recorded with Peter Spilles of Project Pitchfork and reached number one on the DAC.

With the 2009 album “Intoxxication” she focused on further collaborations around the single “Superior Love”, issued in two versions: “The Bright Side”, featuring Limahl with remixes by acts including Real Life and Girls Under Glass, and “The Dark Side”, featuring 18 Summers with contributions from Illuminate and In My Rosary. Between 2011 and 2016 she released a series of duets, including “Where the Wild Roses Grow” and “Jeanny” with forensic biologist Mark Benecke, and “Weg zurück”, “Falling” and “Sie wusste mehr” with Oswald Henke of Goethes Erben. The album “Entre Quatre Yeuxx” was released in 2015.

In 2025 Sara Noxx founded Epixx Studios in Berlin, where she worked on the triptych “Onyxx”, “Polluxx” and “Detoxx”, announced in March 2026 for release via Prussia Records / ZYX. In June 2026, “Poor Old Man” and “Superior Love” placed first and second on the DAC and AAC simultaneously, alongside a digital reissue campaign for “Intoxxication”. “Ultraviolet” now arrives as the lead single from “Onyxx”, the first instalment of that triptych.

items.title: Los Angeles Post-Punk Project Omnihell Shares “Handcuffed to the Steering Wheel” —  Debut Live Show and “Blood Work” EP Announced!
items.summary: I wanted you to notice I have you on a string But if I twist a finger That finger starts to bleed There is a cruel irony in trying to… The post Los Angeles Post-Punk Project Omnihell Shares “Handcuffed to the Steering Wheel” — Debut Live Show and “Blood Work”
items.fullText:
I wanted you to notice
I have you on a string
But if I twist a finger
That finger starts to bleed

There is a cruel irony in trying to hold another person emotionally captive, particularly when the ropes that bind them eventually tighten around your own wrists. Relationships of a toxic nature have a way of becoming elaborate systems of mutual confinement, with both parties convinced they possess the keys, even as the walls slowly close around them.

Los Angeles musician Julian Ash explores that treacherous human appetite for control on Handcuffed to the Steering Wheel, the latest single from his Omnihell project.

The song was written and produced by Ash, with drums by Blake Dimas and mastering by Auragraph. Its jangling guitars and jaunty backbeat establish an unexpectedly buoyant atmosphere, lending the music an almost carefree disposition that sits curiously against its troubled subject matter. The guitars tumble through the arrangement with a delicate, chiming quality, while Dimas maintains a brisk, unhurried rhythm that gives the composition a pleasing sense of forward motion. Beneath this apparent lightness resides a considerably more complicated emotional landscape.

Ash’s vocals are particularly beautiful, delivered with a forlorn tenderness that seems to occupy some distant space between memory and apparition. Generous layers of echo surround his voice, lending each phrase a spectral quality, as though a departed spirit has briefly returned to impart the wisdom acquired through a lifetime of unfortunate decisions. His delivery carries the weary affection of someone who has already experienced the consequences of his mistakes and would dearly prefer that somebody else be spared the same education.

The lyrics examine the uncomfortable relationship between manipulation and vulnerability, beginning with the desire to control another person before gradually revealing the damage such control inflicts upon its wielder. Here is someone ostensibly responsible for determining his own direction, yet physically incapable of abandoning the machinery carrying him forward. The simplicity of the phrases gives them a disturbing authority, particularly when heard against music whose gentle momentum seems almost oblivious to the predicament being described.

Brief but affecting, Handcuffed to the Steering Wheel leaves an impression of emotional exhaustion tempered by considerable compassion. Its modest arrangement, luminous guitar work, and beautifully distant vocals suggest a conversation with the past, conducted in the faint hope that experience might eventually lead to better judgment.

Omnihell will perform live on January 22 at El Cid in Los Angeles, presented by Minty Boi, coinciding with the release of the short EP Bloodwork. Ash plans to perform with a full live band, allowing the songs to develop organically onstage and giving their more fragile emotional qualities room to breathe.

items.fullText:
Cleveland, Ohio’s Frayle will close out 2026 with two Midwest appearances, bringing their collision of towering doom guitars and spectral vocal harmonies to Michigan and Ohio before returning to the studio to write new material. The dates include an October bill with Chicago gothic post-punk duo Bellhead and a December benefit supporting Toys for Tots.

The announcement follows Frayle’s autumn run supporting pagan-metal duo EIHWAR on the Nordic Ritual Nights tour. That stretch of shows came after an earlier interruption to their touring plans: a spring outing with Dogma was cancelled because of international visa processing delays.

At the center of Frayle’s music are vocalist Gwyn Strang and guitarist Sean Bilovecky, whose partnership brings an unusual delicacy to the considerable weight of their arrangements. Strang’s melodies float above low-tuned guitars, drawing out the tension between the intimacy of her delivery and the force beneath it. Doom’s slow, oppressive heft meets the blurred textures of blackgaze, giving their self-described “lullabies of chaos” an appeal that extends into the heavier reaches of gothic music.

Their latest album, Heretics & Lullabies, arrived on October 10, 2025, through Napalm Records. Recorded by Shane Stanton at Glower Studios and produced, mixed, and mastered by Aaron Chaparian at Iron Audio, the ten-track release includes Walking Wounded, their interpretation of Lana Del Rey’s Summertime Sadness, and Heretic.

Listen to Heretics & Lullabies below, and order the album here.

For a further introduction ahead of the shows, revisit the video for Heretic. The album’s penultimate track features guest vocals from Jason Popson, who also appears on Boo.

Frayle’s first date takes place on Friday, October 30, at Small’s in Hamtramck, Michigan, in the Detroit area. Joining Frayle are Bellhead, whose dual-bass approach gives their gothic post-punk a muscular, abrasive edge. Their stripped-down configuration offers a sharp complement to Frayle’s expansive guitar arrangements, with local act Obselite completing the bill.

Frayle’s final appearance of the year follows on Saturday, December 5, at Mercury Music Lounge in Lakewood, Ohio. Co-headlining alongside A Killer’s Confession, the band will take part in the venue’s annual Toys for Tots Drive. Attendees are encouraged to bring a toy donation to help support families in need during the holiday season.

Both shows offer a final opportunity to catch Frayle this year before their attention turns toward writing. Tickets are available through the links below, with capacity limited at each venue.

Between organ crypt and confessions

With ‘Broken Sins’, Vampire Valentine have delivered a real banger that is abso­lutely at home on their latest EP, ‘Scarred And Sacred’. Here, the English band explores the dark­er sides of the human psyche, both music­ally and lyr­ic­ally. At the heart of the song is the story of a man bur­ied under the weight of his sins and past deeds, who pleads daily for for­give­ness for the sal­va­tion of his soul. It’s a lyr­ic­al theme that really gripped me from the very first line.

I’m par­tic­u­larly impressed by the instru­ment­al real­isa­tion of this inner drama. The track picks up the tempo at a pleas­antly brisk pace and imme­di­ately invites you to dance, without los­ing any of its depth. What makes this song so spe­cial to me are the eer­ie organ melod­ies, which sound as though they’ve sprung straight from a clas­sic hor­ror film. Alongside this, care­fully placed syn­thes­iser accents provide strik­ing and clearly aud­ible high­lights. Vampire Valentine demon­strate a keen sense of atmo­sphere here, cre­at­ing a beau­ti­ful, sombre, old-school dark wave sound.

items.title: Noemi Aurora – Kintsugi
items.summary: Album review of Noemi Aurora’s Kintsugi: A dark wave and synth pop masterpiece turning pain into gold. Discover why this solo debut is essential listening.
items.fullText:
Kintsugi: A Shimmering Symphony of Metamorphosis

Album facts

Release Date: February, 7th 2025
Label: Spleen+ / Alfa Matrix
Tags: Dark Wave, Synth Pop
Discogs: Noemi Aurora – Kintsugi
Partially sounds like: Dead Can Dance, Siouxsie, Kate Bush, Ladytron, Front 242, Massive Attack, Cocteau Twins
Final score: 4.67 stars

There are albums you listen to. There are albums you admire. And then, very rarely, there are albums that seem to recog­nize some­thing inside you before you even have found the words for it your­self. « Kintsugi » belongs to that third cat­egory. Noemi Aurora's first solo album does not feel like a con­ven­tion­al debut. It feels more like the open­ing of a sealed cham­ber, a place where elec­tron­ic pulses, noc­turn­al poetry, sen­su­al­ity, vul­ner­ab­il­ity, dark­ness and an almost extra­ter­restri­al sense of beauty have been quietly accu­mu­lat­ing for years.

The title could hardly be more appro­pri­ate. Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repair­ing broken objects while delib­er­ately leav­ing their frac­tures vis­ible. Noemi Aurora takes that philo­sophy and turns it into sound. The cracks are not con­cealed here. They become cir­cuitry. They become veins. They become golden elec­tric­al paths run­ning through every song.

What makes « Kintsugi » par­tic­u­larly fas­cin­at­ing is that it nev­er treats dark­ness as merely some­thing neg­at­ive. Darkness becomes a hab­it­at. A labor­at­ory. Sometimes even a play­ground. This is music for people who have dis­covered that sur­viv­ing some­thing does not neces­sar­ily mean return­ing to who they were before it happened. Sometimes sur­viv­al means becom­ing someone else. And « Kintsugi » is an album about that metamorphosis.

The Sound Of The Album

Noemi Aurora cre­ates a strange ter­rit­ory some­where between dark­wave, elec­tro, indus­tri­al elec­tron­ics, post-punk, synth pop and some­thing far more dif­fi­cult to cat­egor­ize. But genre labels only describe the walls of the room. They don't describe what hap­pens inside it.

Her pro­duc­tion has a par­tic­u­lar noc­turn­al mag­net­ism: syn­thet­ic tex­tures appear cold at first, then gradu­ally reveal warmth under­neath. Percussion can feel mech­an­ic­al while the voice remains intensely human. Melodies some­times seem almost fra­gile before sud­denly acquir­ing an enorm­ous emo­tion­al grav­ity. And then there is her voice. It doesn't simply sit on top of the elec­tron­ics. It moves through them. Sometimes seduct­ive, some­times wounded, some­times com­mand­ing, some­times almost spec­tral, Noemi's voice becomes anoth­er instru­ment, a liv­ing thread con­nect­ing the human body to the album's strange elec­tron­ic uni­verse. That is per­haps the album's greatest achieve­ment : tech­no­logy nev­er man­ages to erase human­ity. Instead, the machines illu­min­ate it.

Keep Your Tears To Water My Roots

The album begins not with an explo­sion, but with an invoc­a­tion. « Keep Your Tears To Water My Roots » imme­di­ately estab­lishes one of Kintsugi's cent­ral ideas: pain doesn't neces­sar­ily have to des­troy us. Sometimes it becomes nour­ish­ment. The imagery of erosion, fall­ing leaves, roots, water and the body cre­ates an almost ele­ment­al atmo­sphere. Nature and emo­tion become impossible to separate.

It feels like watch­ing someone stand­ing inside the ruins of their former self and real­iz­ing that some­thing is still grow­ing there. The song is del­ic­ate without being weak. It is emo­tion­al pho­to­syn­thes­is — sor­row enter­ing the dark­ness and some­how pro­du­cing light. The song intro­duces the album's philo­sophy without explain­ing it. You simply feel it.

Blood As Lipstick

This is one of the album's defin­ing state­ments. The title itself is mag­ni­fi­cent: turn­ing blood, tra­di­tion­ally a sym­bol of injury — into lip­stick, tra­di­tion­ally a sym­bol of beauty, seduc­tion and self-expres­sion. That con­tra­dic­tion is essen­tially « Kintsugi » in mini­ature. This is not a song about pre­tend­ing that wounds don't exist. It is about wear­ing sur­viv­al as decoration.

The song's atti­tude is fierce: pain becomes some­thing con­fron­ted rather than hid­den. The prot­ag­on­ist doesn't ask the dark­ness for per­mis­sion to exist. She walks dir­ectly into it. There is some­thing almost vam­pir­ic about the imagery, but beneath the sen­su­al­ity lies a much more human mes­sage : I have been hurt, but you will not decide what that hurt turns me into. It trans­forms vul­ner­ab­il­ity into defi­ance without sac­ri­fi­cing emo­tion­al depth.

Too Late To Die

One of the most cine­mat­ic pieces on the album. The col­li­sion between Italian verses and the English title cre­ates an espe­cially inter­est­ing sen­sa­tion : some­thing intensely intim­ate sud­denly becomes uni­ver­sal. The song lives some­where between insom­nia, neon, grav­ity and dreams. Its cent­ral para­dox is won­der­ful: it is “too late to die” because some­thing inside the prot­ag­on­ist has already decided to live. The imagery of elec­tric dreams, mag­net­ic fields, fall­ing and an immor­tal heart­beat gives the song an almost urb­an-super­nat­ur­al qual­ity. It feels like run­ning through a sleep­ing city at 3 a.m. with the ter­ri­fy­ing real­iz­a­tion that you are still alive and that per­haps you have nev­er felt more alive. It turns sur­viv­al into exhilaration.

Shining

« Shining » is the album's neon heart­beat. The melody of this song reminds me so much of « Fade To Grey » by Visage. It is imme­di­ately access­ible, but its appar­ent sim­pli­city hides a dark­er archi­tec­ture. Mirrors, roses, wounds, dark­ness, stars and the destruc­tion of the sun all coex­ist inside a song that man­ages to be dance­able without becom­ing emo­tion­ally light­weight. That is dif­fi­cult to accom­plish. The title sounds optim­ist­ic. The song isn't entirely optim­ist­ic. And that ten­sion is exactly what makes it fascinating.

This is lumin­oir, a kind of dark­ness that doesn't extin­guish light but makes the light more vis­ible. « Shining » doesn't say that everything is beau­ti­ful. It says that beauty can con­tin­ue to exist even when some­thing has cracked. This song is prob­ably the clearest son­ic mani­festo of the entire album.

Malicious Logic

Here the album becomes more con­front­a­tion­al. « Malicious Logic » feels like an inter­rog­a­tion of guilt, memory, desire and the strange ways people ration­al­ize what they have done. The song's elec­tron­ic pulse gives those ques­tions a phys­ic­al dimen­sion. You don't merely hear the repe­ti­tion. You feel trapped inside it. The phrase “mali­cious logic” itself sug­gests a dis­turb­ing mech­an­ism : the human mind con­struct­ing per­fectly con­vin­cing explan­a­tions for things that per­haps should nev­er have happened. There is some­thing almost cyber­net­ic about the song's psy­cho­logy. A con­science with a syn­thes­izer attached to it. And that is one of its greatest strengths.

Animal

« Animal » is instinct return­ing to the body. After the psy­cho­lo­gic­al ten­sion of « Malicious Logic », this track feels more phys­ic­al, more prim­al. The mes­sage is essen­tially : stop overthink­ing for a moment. Move. Breathe. Fight. Try again. The phrase “CTRL+ALT+TRY AGAIN” is par­tic­u­larly effect­ive because it trans­lates emo­tion­al rebirth into com­puter language.

A restart. A reboot. Another attempt. But under­neath the tech­no­lo­gic­al imagery is some­thing pro­foundly prim­it­ive : the refus­al to sur­render. This is sur­viv­al code dis­guised as a dance track. It recon­nects the album's cereb­ral elec­tron­ic world with some­thing instinct­ive and bodily.

Dal Giardino Di Algos

One of the album's most mys­ter­i­ous pieces — and, for me, one of its most fas­cin­at­ing. The Italian lan­guage changes the emo­tion­al tem­per­at­ure imme­di­ately. There is some­thing almost ritu­al­ist­ic about « Dal Giardino Di Algos ». The “garden” isn't neces­sar­ily a peace­ful place. It feels like a for­bid­den land­scape where beauty and danger grow from the same soil.

The song seems to des­cend rather than simply pro­gress. It is sen­su­al, fever­ish and strangely myth­o­lo­gic­al. And the Italian vocals make it feel even more intim­ate, as though the listen­er has acci­dent­ally over­heard a private incant­a­tion. This is not simply a song. It feels like a ritu­al­o­gram, an emo­tion­al ritu­al writ­ten in sound. It gives « Kintsugi » an almost occult dimen­sion without becom­ing the­at­ric­al for the sake of it.

Bring Me The Lake

This is where beauty becomes dan­ger­ous. The lake is sim­ul­tan­eously attract­ive and threat­en­ing. Nature isn't presen­ted as a com­fort­ing refuge; it pos­sesses secrets, dark­ness and destruct­ive power. That con­tra­dic­tion is extraordin­ary. The song asks us to move closer to some­thing even though we know it may hurt us. And isn't that one of the great con­tra­dic­tions of human desire?

We fre­quently approach the things we know can con­sume us. « Bring Me The Lake » feels like stand­ing at the edge of an unknown body of water at night and real­iz­ing that the fear is pre­cisely what makes you want to enter. The song cre­ates one of the album's most vivid cine­mat­ic environments.

The Alchemist

If « Kintsugi » is about trans­form­ing dam­age into beauty, « The Alchemist » is prac­tic­ally its philo­soph­ic­al center­piece, the album's clearest state­ment of its cent­ral philo­sophy. The song rejects the con­ven­tion­al savior nar­rat­ive. There is no need for a hero. No need for someone else to arrive and repair everything. Instead, trans­form­a­tion becomes an act of per­son­al chem­istry. The scars remain. The ruins remain. But some­thing new can be cre­ated from them. The imagery of pois­on, crowns, ruins, rain, rivers and dia­monds makes the song feel almost like a goth­ic fairy tale for adults.

And the final concept is beau­ti­ful : someone tak­ing broken dreams and trans­form­ing them into some­thing pre­cious. That is Kintsugi. Not eras­ing the frac­ture. Changing what the frac­ture means.

Stranger To Myself

This is one of the album's most psy­cho­lo­gic­ally intim­ate moments. The song con­fronts that fright­en­ing exper­i­ence of no longer recog­niz­ing your­self — and then dis­cov­er­ing that per­haps the per­son you were hid­ing from was your­self all along. The emo­tion­al move­ment is import­ant. It doesn't simply remain in ali­en­a­tion. It moves toward recog­ni­tion. Toward reclaim­ing the self, trans­form­ing iden­tity crisis into self-recov­ery. There is some­thing incred­ibly human about that. The title begins as a con­fes­sion. By the end, it feels almost like a dia­gnos­is that has been over­turned. I am no longer a stranger to myself. That makes the song feel like one of the album's emo­tion­al turn­ing points.

Untouchable

Dreamlike, sen­su­al and slightly dan­ger­ous. « Untouchable » feels as though real­ity has become unstable. There are shad­ows, spir­its, magic doors, white horses, altern­ate dimen­sions and the idea of exist­ing some­where out­side ordin­ary rules. The title is par­tic­u­larly clev­er because the song itself is full of intim­acy. The nar­rat­or wants close­ness while sim­ul­tan­eously remain­ing unreach­able. That con­tra­dic­tion gives the song its erot­ic ten­sion. It is desire with an escape route built into it. A love song for people who live halfway between real­ity and fantasy.

Yugen

The per­fect clos­ing state­ment. « Yugen » is a Japanese aes­thet­ic concept asso­ci­ated with pro­found, mys­ter­i­ous beauty — some­thing that can­not be com­pletely explained, only felt. That makes the title extraordin­ar­ily appro­pri­ate for the end of « Kintsugi ». After all the blood, wounds, desire, dark­ness, move­ment and trans­form­a­tion, the album doesn't con­clude with a gigant­ic explo­sion. It dis­solves. The song reaches toward radi­ance and some­thing almost divine, but nev­er com­pletely explains what that radi­ance is. And per­haps that is exactly the point.

Some exper­i­ences lose their magic when you explain them. Some things should remain partly hid­den. « Yugen » leaves the door open. And when the final echoes dis­ap­pear, « Kintsugi » doesn't feel fin­ished. It feels unfin­ished in the most beau­ti­ful pos­sible way. It doesn't close the story. It leaves the listen­er sus­pen­ded inside it.

In Conclusion

« Kintsugi » is not an album that asks to be con­sumed quickly. It asks to be entered. Its songs behave less like isol­ated tracks and more like rooms in the same strange house.

Some are neon-lit. Some are flooded. Some con­tain mir­rors. Some con­tain wounds. Some con­tain mon­sters. Some con­tain gar­dens. And some­where inside all of them is the same ques­tion : what if being broken isn't the oppos­ite of being beau­ti­ful? Noemi Aurora's answer is not delivered as a slo­gan. It is delivered through rhythm, cir­cuitry, poetry, sen­su­al­ity, dis­tor­tion, silence and voice.

That is why « Kintsugi » feels much lar­ger than a debut album. It feels like an auto­bi­o­graphy writ­ten in elec­tri­city. A scar-sym­phony. A noc­turn­al meta­morph­os­is. A gold-threaded nervous sys­tem. And per­haps most import­antly, it is an album that refuses to apo­lo­gise for its dark­ness. It doesn't ask dark­ness to become light. It teaches dark­ness how to glow.

This is the very first time I give such a high rat­ing to an album. Musically per­fect, I can tell that Noemi Aurora spent an insane amount of time on the com­pos­i­tion of the melod­ies. Lyrically inspired, the verses carry such deep mean­ing and even have sev­er­al levels of under­stand­ing. And on top of all that, there’s the voice of Noemi Aurora.

How in the world is it pos­sible to have such a pure and addict­ive voice which car­ries so much fra­gil­ity and raw power at the same time? I strongly recom­mend this album with all my heart and soul ! I won’t go in details, but simply know that it has done touched me on a very deep level, brought me strength, com­fort, cour­age,… much more than any oth­er album I have ever listened to. This is essen­tial listen­ing for any­one who believes that music should do more than enter­tain, it should alter the tem­per­at­ure of the soul.

Find the exclus­ive inter­view with Noemi Aurora in our Print-Magazine issue #03.

items.fullText:
When the cold takes over

For me, the intro to “Too Far Gone” alone has it all. A thick bass­line meets cool, clas­sic ana­logue synth sounds, giv­ing the whole track an incred­ibly rich and elec­tron­ic sound. Only the subtly inter­woven gui­tar, which skil­fully drifts from the left to the right chan­nel, adds a subtle touch of dark wave.

But that’s only half the story, because the vocals are also out­stand­ing, pleas­antly soft and a per­fect fit for this sombre vibe. When the chor­us kicks in, it really gives me goose­bumps. Accompanied by lines about speech­less­ness and emo­tion­al cold­ness, in which a mouth­ful of dag­gers and icy bones fall on deaf ears, this unfolds into a lyr­ic­ally power­ful track.

items.title: Korfian – Melodramatic
items.summary: With ‘Melodramatic’, Korfian presents a brilliant electro track full of character. An eccentric sonic experience without the drama.
items.fullText:
When silence is frightening: Korfian and the art of electronic catharsis

The sound of Korfian’s new single ‘Melodramatic’ is fant­ast­ic­ally elec­tron­ic, as if Björk’s Greek cous­in were at the con­trols, so to speak. Musically, the track oper­ates in the realm of elec­tro (with a touch of synth pop?) and comes across as pleas­antly exper­i­ment­al, but to my taste it stays firmly on track son­ic­ally, without drift­ing into any­thing too com­plex or wild. It’s a very dis­tinct­ive elec­tro sound that doesn’t quite fit into the clas­sic synth-pop mould styl­ist­ic­ally. Whether you find the whole thing unwieldy or catchy prob­ably depends on your own listen­ing habits.

In any case, the song com­pletely won me over from the very first listen. Lyrically, Korfian takes aim at staged suf­fer­ing and tox­ic dynam­ics with his usu­al pre­ci­sion. A cath­artic act of lib­er­a­tion, wrapped in an express­ive elec­tron­ic guise.
